For people in high-risk communities, securing the home network is important to stop threat actors from getting into the network and reading any unencrypted data that is sent over it. A router lets your phones, laptops, desktop computers, and smart devices connect wirelessly to the internet, and this guide helps you change common router settings to improve privacy and security.

Router Settings Essential for Your Cybersecurity
At a minimum, you must ensure that you take the following steps to protect your network’s
security:
1. Change your router login username and password.
Your default </resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary> router information may be
publicly available for anyone to find, so it is crucial to change your credentials. Create a
password that is long, random, and unique.
2. Check your router firmware for updates.
Routine updates will protect you against known vulnerabilities. Some routers even allow
you to set up automatic updates. 
3. Change your default SSID.
In other words, change the name of your Wi-Fi network. The default SSID could potentially
alert a threat actor to known vulnerabilities </resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary>
associated with the router you are using. (Note:Do not give your Wi-Fi network a name that
includes sensitive or identifying personal information.)
4. Change your Wi-Fi password.
This is the password that someone must enter to access your Wi-Fi. To make your Wi-Fi
password both secure and accessible, try creating a memorable passphrase using 5 to 7
unrelated words totaling at least 16 characters. Do not use this passphrase for other
accounts. 
5. Change your Wi-Fi encryption.
Check to make sure your router uses WPA3 Personal or WPA2 AES (also referred to as WPA2
Pre-Shared Key [PSK] or WPA2) encryption. These are the only two forms of encryption that
are considered safe and secure against threat actors who might attempt to see what data

encryption and is not secure), or uses an older generation of encryption such as WEP, WPA,
or WPA2 Temporary Key Integrity Protocol (TKIP), you should contact the internet service
provider </resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary> (ISP) that provided your router to
request an upgrade ― or consider purchasing a new router.
6. Disable remote management.
This setting allows you to log in to your router over the internet to make changes. Disabling
this setting can prevent threat actors from making changes to your router without
connecting to your network first, either wirelessly or via cable.
7. Disable Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS).
This setting increases the likelihood that a threat actor could gain unauthorized access to
your Wi-Fi network. See CISA's blog on Home Network Security <https://www.cisa.gov/newsevents/news/home-network-security> to learn more.
8. Disable Universal Plug and Play (UPnP).
UPnP allows you to easily connect smart devices in your home (e.g., your smart speaker or
dishwasher) to your Wi-Fi network. However, threat actors can use UPnP to spread malware
</resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary> to devices in your network and control them
remotely. (See CISA’s blog on Home Network Security <https://www.cisa.gov/newsevents/news/home-network-security> to learn more.) In some cases, you may need to enable
UPnP to initially add your device to the network, but you should disable UPnP after doing
so.
9. Store your router in a secure physical location.
Anyone with physical access to your router could perform a factory reset and use the
default information displayed on the router to gain access to the network.
10. Create a “Guest” Wi-Fi option.

reference: TheMoon malware was first discovered on compromised routers in 2014 and has since gone through several campaigns.
reference_contexts:
Alert Number: I-050725-PSA
May 7, 2025
 Cyber Criminal Proxy Services Exploiting End of Life Routers
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is issuing this announcement to inform
individuals and businesses about proxy services taking advantage of end of life
routers that are susceptible to vulnerabilities. When a hardware device is end of
life, the manufacturer no longer sells the product and is not actively supporting the
hardware, which also means they are no longer releasing software updates or
security patches for the device. Routers dated 2010 or earlier likely no longer
receive software updates issued by the manufacturer and could be compromised by
cyber actors exploiting known vulnerabilities.
End of life routers were breached by cyber actors using variants of TheMoon
malware botnet. Recently, some routers at end of life, with remote administration
turned on, were identified as compromised by a new variant of TheMoon malware.
This malware allows cyber actors to install proxies on unsuspecting victim routers
and conduct cyber crimes anonymously.
 PROXIES AND ROUTER VULNERABILITIES
A proxy server is a system or router that provides a gateway between users and
the Internet. It is an intermediary between end-users and the web pages they visit
online. A proxy is a service that relays users' Internet traffic while hiding the link
between users and their activity.
Cyber actors use proxy services to hide their identities and location. When actors
use a proxy service to visit a website to conduct criminal activity, like stealing
cryptocurrency or contracting illegal services, the website does not register their
real IP address and instead registers the proxy IP.
 THEMOON MALWARE
TheMoon malware was first discovered on compromised routers in 2014 and has
since gone through several campaigns. TheMoon does not require a password to
infect routers; it scans for open ports and sends a command to a vulnerable script.
The malware contacts the command and control (C2) server and the C2 server
responds with instructions, which may include instructing the infected machine to
scan for other vulnerable routers to spread the infection and expand the network.
 TIPS TO PROTECT YOURSELF

Commonly identified signs of malware infections on routers include overheating
devices, problems with connectivity, and changes to settings the administrator
does not recognize.
The FBI recommends individuals and companies take the following precautions:
If the router is at end of life, replace the device with an updated model if
possible.
Immediately apply any available security patches and/or firmware updates for

Login online to the router settings and disable remote management/remote
administration, save the change, and reboot the router.
Use strong passwords that are unique and random and contain at least 16 but
no more than 64 characters. Avoid reusing passwords and disable password

If you believe there is suspicious activity on any device, apply any necessary

user_input: How does CVSS version 4.0 use its different metric groups to calculate and communicate the severity of a software vulnerability?
reference: According to the CVSS version 4.0 User Guide, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) is an open framework for communicating the characteristics and severity of software vulnerabilities. CVSS consists of four metric groups: Base, Threat, Environmental, and Supplemental. The Base group represents the intrinsic qualities of a vulnerability that are constant over time and across user environments. The Threat group reflects the characteristics of a vulnerability that change over time. The Environmental group represents the characteristics of a vulnerability that are unique to a user's environment. Base metric values are combined with default values that assume the highest severity for Threat and Environmental metrics to produce a score ranging up to 10. To further refine a resulting severity score, Threat and Environmental metrics can then be amended based on applicable threat intelligence and environmental considerations. Supplemental metrics do not modify the final score, and are used as additional insight into the characteristics of a vulnerability. A CVSS vector string consists of a compressed textual representation of the values used to derive the score.

user_input: What does a CVSS-B (base) score tell me about a vulnerability — just how severe it is, or the real-world risk too?
reference: In CVSS version 4.0, CVSS-B refers to a score calculated using only the Base metrics. The CVSS Specification Document explains that CVSS Base (CVSS-B) scores are designed to measure the severity of a vulnerability and should not be used alone to assess risk. The Base Score represents only the intrinsic characteristics of a vulnerability and is independent of any factor associated with threat or the computing environment where the vulnerable system resides. To get closer to a measure of risk, the Base Score should be supplemented with an analysis of the environment (Environmental Metrics) and with attributes that may change over time (Threat Metrics), which together can produce a CVSS-BTE score that is considered much closer to risk.

user_input: As a tech‑curious home user, how should I handle my router’s SSID to improve security, and how does properly managing the SSID work together with other key router settings like changing default credentials and using strong Wi‑Fi encryption to reduce the risk that threat actors can access or exploit my home network?
reference:
The SSID is the service set identifier, or the name of your Wi‑Fi network, and handling it correctly is an important part of securing your home router.

From the initial setup perspective, your router may have a sticker that lists default information such as the IP address, SSID, key (password), MAC address, and account name. Using this default information as‑is is risky, because default router information may be publicly available for anyone to find. That means a threat actor could use widely known default settings to try to access your router and your network.

To address this, one of the essential router settings for cybersecurity is to change your default SSID. In other words, you should change the default Wi‑Fi network name that came with the router. Leaving the default SSID in place can potentially alert a threat actor to known vulnerabilities associated with the specific router you are using, because the default name often reveals the brand and model. When you pick a new SSID, you should also avoid using sensitive or identifying personal information in the name.

Managing the SSID works best when combined with several other key security steps on the router:

1. Change your router login username and password. Because default router information may be publicly available, it is crucial to change these credentials and create a password that is long, random, and unique. This helps prevent someone from logging into the router’s settings, even if they know the default information printed on the device.

2. Change your Wi‑Fi password. This is the password people must enter to join your Wi‑Fi network (associated with the SSID). It should be a secure but memorable passphrase using 5 to 7 unrelated words totaling at least 16 characters, and it should not be reused for other accounts.

3. Change your Wi‑Fi encryption to a secure option. You should configure the router to use WPA3 Personal or WPA2 AES (also called WPA2 Pre‑Shared Key or WPA2). These encryption types are considered safe against threat actors who might attempt to see what data you are sending across your network. If the router is open (no encryption) or uses older options like WEP, WPA, or WPA2 TKIP, you should request an upgraded router from your internet service provider or consider purchasing a new one.

4. Apply other essential protections, such as disabling remote management, disabling WPS and UPnP when possible, storing the router in a secure physical location, and using a separate Guest Wi‑Fi network for visitors and certain smart home or IoT devices.

Taken together, properly managing your SSID (by changing the default name and avoiding personal details), along with changing default router credentials, setting a strong Wi‑Fi password, and enabling strong encryption, significantly reduces the chances that threat actors can identify your router model, leverage known vulnerabilities, or gain unauthorized access to your home network and the data you send over it.

you adjust settings that are common to all routers for better privacy and security.
Setting Up
Before you make any changes to your network, here are a few quick tips and facts to make
the process easier:
Note: Each router is different. For a step-by-step guide to performing these instructions,
please refer to your own router’s user guide.
1. Find your router. It may have a sticker on it with the default setting information. While
this information may vary, it typically includes the following:
a. IP address </resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary>
b. Service set identifier (SSID) </resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary>
c. Key (password)
d. MAC address </resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary>
e. Account name
2. To access your router, reference the manufacturer’s user manual and follow directions
for making changes to the settings described below.

Router Settings Essential for Your Cybersecurity
At a minimum, you must ensure that you take the following steps to protect your network’s
security:
1. Change your router login username and password.
Your default </resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary> router information may be
publicly available for anyone to find, so it is crucial to change your credentials. Create a
password that is long, random, and unique.
2. Check your router firmware for updates.
Routine updates will protect you against known vulnerabilities. Some routers even allow
you to set up automatic updates. 
3. Change your default SSID.
In other words, change the name of your Wi-Fi network. The default SSID could potentially
alert a threat actor to known vulnerabilities </resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary>
associated with the router you are using. (Note:Do not give your Wi-Fi network a name that
includes sensitive or identifying personal information.)
4. Change your Wi-Fi password.
This is the password that someone must enter to access your Wi-Fi. To make your Wi-Fi
password both secure and accessible, try creating a memorable passphrase using 5 to 7
unrelated words totaling at least 16 characters. Do not use this passphrase for other
accounts. 
5. Change your Wi-Fi encryption.
Check to make sure your router uses WPA3 Personal or WPA2 AES (also referred to as WPA2
Pre-Shared Key [PSK] or WPA2) encryption. These are the only two forms of encryption that
are considered safe and secure against threat actors who might attempt to see what data

https://www.cisa.gov/audiences/high-risk-communities/projectupskill/module5 3/7
you are sending across your network. If your router is open (meaning it doesn’t have
encryption and is not secure), or uses an older generation of encryption such as WEP, WPA,
or WPA2 Temporary Key Integrity Protocol (TKIP), you should contact the internet service
provider </resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary> (ISP) that provided your router to
request an upgrade ― or consider purchasing a new router.
6. Disable remote management.
This setting allows you to log in to your router over the internet to make changes. Disabling
this setting can prevent threat actors from making changes to your router without
connecting to your network first, either wirelessly or via cable.
7. Disable Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS).
This setting increases the likelihood that a threat actor could gain unauthorized access to
your Wi-Fi network. See CISA's blog on Home Network Security <https://www.cisa.gov/newsevents/news/home-network-security> to learn more.
8. Disable Universal Plug and Play (UPnP).
UPnP allows you to easily connect smart devices in your home (e.g., your smart speaker or
dishwasher) to your Wi-Fi network. However, threat actors can use UPnP to spread malware
</resources-tools/resources/project-upskill-glossary> to devices in your network and control them
remotely. (See CISA’s blog on Home Network Security <https://www.cisa.gov/newsevents/news/home-network-security> to learn more.) In some cases, you may need to enable
UPnP to initially add your device to the network, but you should disable UPnP after doing
so.
9. Store your router in a secure physical location.
Anyone with physical access to your router could perform a factory reset and use the
default information displayed on the router to gain access to the network.
10. Create a “Guest” Wi-Fi option.

that is long, random, and unique for accessing your Guest Wi-Fi.
1. Your Guest Wi-Fi should be used by anyone who does not routinely connect to your
home Wi-Fi.
2. Additionally, connect any smart home and other IOT </resources-tools/resources/projectupskill-glossary> devices to your Guest Wi-Fi if internet access is the only thing they
require. This will prevent these devices from discovering other devices on your home
network, accessing your router settings, and potentially introducing vulnerabilities into
your network.

user_input: As a home user, how does the Broadband Forum guidance fit into the cybersecurity advice for consumer-grade routers, and what kinds of protections and other standards does NIST say should be used alongside the Broadband Forum recommendations to keep my router and its logs secure?
reference:
The Broadband Forum guidance is one of the key standards that NIST recommends manufacturers use when they design consumer-grade routers. Specifically, NIST points to the Broadband Forum (BBF) TR-124 Issue 8, which sets functional requirements for broadband residential gateway devices. This BBF standard is one of four existing router standards that NIST recommends as a starting point for technical capabilities on router devices.

NIST explains that requirements from these four router standards (including the Broadband Forum one) mainly focus on the router device itself and describe many cybersecurity capabilities that are appropriate for this equipment. NIST notes that most of the requirements from these standards are unique and that they give useful detail on how to meet cybersecurity outcomes and which cybersecurity features should be included in consumer-grade routers.

Alongside the Broadband Forum guidance, NIST recommends additional protections and standards to improve router cybersecurity and to keep important data like logs secure:

- For router logs and cybersecurity state information, NIST highlights the need for robust security, such as encrypting and password protecting logs so that only authorized people can access them, using non-volatile memory storage for logs, using off-device storage for logged data, and restricting log deletion. These measures help protect logs, which are valuable for detecting compromised routers and for forensic analysis of cybersecurity incidents.

- In addition to the four router-focused standards (which include the Broadband Forum TR-124), NIST recommends using several other publications to fill gaps, especially for non-technical outcomes and for components beyond the router device itself, such as backends or mobile applications. These include Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines (SP 800-193), Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices (SP 800-161 Rev. 1), the Secure Software Development Framework (SP 800-218), and ISO and other guidelines for vulnerability disclosure, vulnerability handling, risk management, and design and development of information for users.

Taken together, the Broadband Forum standard provides part of the functional and technical foundation for router security, while NIST’s broader set of recommended standards and practices (including specific protections for log data) is meant to help manufacturers build more secure consumer-grade routers and handle cybersecurity for the entire product, not just the router box itself.

user_input: If I am at home and want to keep my information safe, how should I think about TLS when my router is talking to websites and when my email program is talking to my mail server, and what simple steps should I take with my router and my own online behavior so that TLS really protects my data instead of me accidentally exposing it?
reference:
TLS is used in two important ways in the context you are given: between your browser and web sites, and between your email program and your mail server.

From the router side, the guidance says that when data are sent between consumer-grade router product components or outside the product, strong protections such as FIPS‑approved algorithms should be used for data transmission. For data related to managing the product, this specifically includes using hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP) over transport layer security (TLS) for external communications via the consumer‑grade router product and for using device management interfaces or web portals. This means that when you log in to manage your router through a web page, that page should use HTTP over TLS so the management traffic is encrypted in transit.

From your own online behavior side, the guidance tells you to always use secure email protocols, particularly if you are using a wireless network. You should configure your email client to use the transport layer security (TLS) option (Secure IMAP or Secure POP3) so that your email is encrypted in transit between the mail server and your device. It also recommends upgrading to a modern browser and keeping it up to date, and watching for indicators in the browser’s URL bar that transit security is in place, which helps protect the confidentiality of your sensitive information over the Internet.

To make TLS really protect your data in practice, you should therefore: ensure your router uses HTTP over TLS for its external management web pages, enable the TLS options (Secure IMAP or Secure POP3) in your email program so your email traffic is encrypted, use a modern, up‑to‑date browser that signals when secure connections are in use, and combine this with the other basic safeguards described, such as avoiding suspicious links and attachments, using strong unique passwords and a password manager, enabling strong authentication on your router, and using multi‑factor authentication where possible. All of these steps together help keep the TLS‑protected connections effective in protecting your data in transit.

user_input: Why should I turn off remote management, WPS, and UPnP on my home router, and how does that keep my network safer?
reference:
You should turn off remote management, WPS setup, and UPnP because they are convenient but make your home Wi-Fi less secure.

From the first part, remote management lets you change your router settings over the internet, WPS lets you push a button on the router to connect a device without typing the Wi-Fi password, and UPnP lets devices find each other on your network. These features can make it easier to add devices or let guests use your Wi-Fi, but they also weaken your network security.

The second part says you should disable the ability to perform remote administration on the routing device and disable UPnP so that attackers have fewer ways to compromise your network. The third part repeats this as simple advice: it tells you to disable remote management, disable WPS setup, and disable UPnP as key takeaways for securing your home Wi-Fi.

Putting these pieces together, turning off remote management, WPS, and UPnP closes extra ways for hackers or malicious software to get into your router and devices, which helps keep your home network safer.

user_input: For a tech-curious home user, why do multiple best-practice guides recommend disabling risky features like remote management, WPS setup, and UPnP on home routers, and how should these be turned off and limited according to the combined guidance from the FTC, NSA, and CISA?
reference:
Multiple best-practice guides recommend disabling features like remote management, WPS, and UPnP because, while convenient, they create additional ways an attacker can reach or manipulate your home network.

From the FTC guidance (<1-hop>), remote management, Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) are identified as features that "can be convenient but weaken your network security." Remote management allows you to change router settings over the internet; if an attacker can reach that interface, they could change settings (including your Wi-Fi password) and undermine other protections. WPS lets you connect devices by pushing a button instead of entering the Wi‑Fi password, and UPnP lets devices automatically find each other on the network. The FTC notes that these can make it easier to add devices or let guests use Wi‑Fi, "but they can make your network less secure." As part of overall router hardening, the FTC explicitly advises turning these features off.

The NSA home network best-practices document (<2-hop>) reinforces this by recommending you "Disable the ability to perform remote administration on the routing device" and "Disable Universal Plug-n-Play (UPnP)." It explains that administration should be limited to the internal network only and that turning off remote administration and UPnP "help close holes that may enable an attacker to compromise your network." This frames these features as potential entry points that can be probed or abused from outside.

CISA’s Project Upskill checklist (<3-hop>) then summarizes these points into concrete to‑dos: under "Do," it lists "Disable remote management," "Disable WPS setup," and "Disable UPnP" alongside other core security steps like changing default credentials, using WPA3 or WPA2 AES, and creating a guest Wi‑Fi. Grouping them with those essential tasks signals that disabling these risky features is a standard, baseline hardening step rather than an optional tweak.

Taken together, the combined guidance from the FTC, NSA, and CISA explains both the "why" and the "how": these features increase your attack surface by exposing configuration access (remote management) and automatically opening connectivity paths between devices and the outside world (UPnP, WPS). To follow best practice, you should:
- Turn off or disable remote management/remote administration so router changes can only be made from inside your home network.
- Disable WPS setup so devices must join the Wi‑Fi using the secure Wi‑Fi password instead of push‑button pairing.
- Disable UPnP so devices cannot silently open paths or discover each other in ways that could be abused.

All three sources agree that disabling these features is part of a basic, recommended configuration for securing a home router.

user_input: How do I make strong, unique passwords for my Wi-Fi and other accounts, and how do password managers help?
reference:
To make strong and unique passwords for your Wi-Fi and other accounts, you should avoid anything easy to guess, like your name, address, router brand, or other personal details. Your router needs two different passwords: one strong, unique Wi-Fi password so strangers cannot join your network, and a separate strong, unique router admin password so a hacker cannot get into the settings and change things.

For all your accounts, passwords should be strong, unique for each account, and difficult to guess. You should not store them in plain text where someone else or malicious software might see them. A password manager is highly recommended because it lets you use long, complex, unique passwords for every account without having to remember them all yourself. It can create and remember strong, unique passwords for you, and you then only need to remember one main password for the manager.

You should also protect answers to password recovery or challenge questions, since they work like passwords. Consider using unique, memorable answers that are not real personal facts an attacker could guess from your life. Avoid letting websites or programs remember passwords directly in the browser; instead, use your password manager to fill them in. Using strong passwords, keeping the Wi-Fi and router admin passwords different and hard to guess, and relying on a password manager to handle complex, unique passwords for each account all work together to improve your overall password strength and security.
